summary: KS3 pupils extend the KS2 term-to-term idea to the position-to-term (nth-term) rule, which gives any term directly from its position. The core moves: generate the SAME sequence two ways (chaining from the previous term vs substituting n=1,2,3,… into a formula like 3n−2); and classify sequences as arithmetic (constant difference), geometric (constant ratio) or other by explicitly writing the successive differences AND successive ratios. Key pitfalls to address: reading 3n−2 as a term-to-term instruction ('start at 3, subtract 2'), classifying by 'it goes up' alone, and confusing 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3'.
misconceptions: Treating a position-to-term rule as a term-to-term instruction (reading 3n−2 as 'start at 3, subtract 2'), so the first term is wrong.
Classifying by 'it goes up' alone, failing to distinguish arithmetic from geometric or to spot a non-constant difference (1, 4, 9, 16).
Assuming a later term can be reached by multiplying an earlier one (10th term = 2 × 5th term).

activities.title: Dual-engine generator: the same sequence built two ways
steps: Build a sequence term-to-term: set a start value and an operation (e.g. start at 1, add 3) and generate the chain one step at a time.
Build the same sequence position-to-term: type a rule such as 3n−2 and substitute n=1,2,3,4,5 to light up each term under its position.
Switch a sequence between the two modes and confirm the numbers are identical.
Press 'jump to the 50th term': in position-to-term mode the answer for 3n−2 appears at once; in term-to-term mode the machine visibly grinds through the 49 predecessors first.
Drag the coefficient of n in 3n−2 and watch the inter-term step change to match, so the coefficient is seen to equal the common difference.
activities.insight: A term-to-term rule chains from the previous term; a position-to-term rule substitutes the position number into a formula and so reaches any term (e.g. the 50th) directly without listing the earlier ones. In a linear rule such as 3n−2 (of the form an + b), the coefficient of n equals the common difference.

activities.title: Classify by writing differences AND ratios
steps: For each sequence, write the row of successive differences and the row of successive ratios underneath it.
Sort sequences into arithmetic (constant difference), geometric (constant ratio) or other (neither constant).
Work the worked set: 5, 8, 11, 14 (arithmetic, difference +3); 2, 6, 18, 54 (geometric, ratio ×3); 1, 4, 9, 16 (other — differences 3, 5, 7 not constant, ratios not constant).
State explicitly which row you checked to make each decision, so classification is a test rather than a guess.

Construct your own sequence of a requested type (for example a geometric sequence that starts at 5, with a ratio other than 1) and verify it with the differences and ratios rows. Note that a constant sequence such as 5, 5, 5 has both a constant difference (0) and a constant ratio (1), so it is both arithmetic and geometric.
activities.insight: A sequence is arithmetic when the successive differences are constant and geometric when the successive ratios are constant; 'it goes up' is not enough, because 1, 4, 9, 16 increases but has a changing difference. The same differences/ratios test can be used to build and check a sequence of a requested type.

activities.title: 'Multiples of 3' versus 'increases by 3'
steps: Check each sequence against the 3-times table and record which terms are multiples of 3.
Explain why 1, 4, 7, 10 increases by 3 yet contains no multiples of 3.
activities.insight: A sequence that increases by 3 need not be the multiples-of-3 sequence; the constant difference (+3) and membership of the 3-times table are different properties.

activities.title: Which rule reaches the 50th term faster, and why? (discussion)
steps: Discuss with a partner (or a questioning prompt): to find the 50th term of 3n−2, which rule gets you there faster — term-to-term or position-to-term — and why?
Articulate that substitution reaches any term directly while chaining requires all earlier terms.

Challenge the claim '10th term = 2 × 5th term' and test it against an actual arithmetic sequence with a nonzero constant term, such as 3n−2. Then notice that it does happen to hold for 3n, so one example that works does not prove the general claim.
activities.insight: The position-to-term rule is powerful because it gives any term directly; you cannot in general reach a later term by multiplying an earlier one (doubling the 5th term does not in general give the 10th: it fails for 3n−2, although it happens to work for rules with no constant term, such as 3n).

activities.title: Practice set: generate, fill and match
steps: Generate the first five terms of a position-to-term rule such as 3n−2 by substitution (fill in the blanks).
Sort a mixed set of sequences into arithmetic / geometric / other.
Match each nth-term rule to the sequence it produces.
activities.insight: Fluency in substituting positions into a rule and in categorising sequences by the correct test.

checkQuestion: Generate the first five terms of the sequence whose rule is 3n − 2. Then look at these three sequences — 5, 8, 11, 14, …; 2, 6, 18, 54, …; 1, 4, 9, 16, … — and sort each as arithmetic, geometric or neither, showing me how you decide.
checkAnswer: 3n−2 gives 1, 4, 7, 10, 13 (substituting n = 1,2,3,4,5). 5, 8, 11, 14 is arithmetic (constant difference +3); 2, 6, 18, 54 is geometric (constant ratio ×3); 1, 4, 9, 16 is neither (differences 3, 5, 7 — not constant; ratios not constant). The child decides by checking the successive differences and the successive ratios.
